client: I've been really struggling lately trying to keep everything together while my partner is away on this work trip. Between putting in full days at the marketing firm and then coming home to take care of our two kids completely on my own, I'm just constantly exhausted and on edge. I honestly don't know if talking about it is going to make any real difference, but I figured I had to try something because I can't keep going like this.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying an enormous amount right now — holding down a demanding job and parenting solo is genuinely exhausting, and it makes complete sense that you're feeling worn thin. I'm really glad you decided to reach out, and I want you to know that talking *can* make a real difference, even when it's hard to believe that in the thick of it. What do you think feels like the heaviest part of it all — is it more the physical tiredness, or is there a particular worry or thought that keeps circling in your mind?

client: Honestly, it's less the physical tiredness and more this thought that just won't leave me alone — that I'm somehow failing my kid because I'm so stretched thin all the time. Like, I'll be at work trying to focus, and this voice in my head keeps saying he deserves more than what I'm giving him. It's exhausting in a way that sleep doesn't really fix.
therapist: That kind of thought — the quiet, persistent voice telling you you're not enough — can be so draining precisely because it follows you everywhere, even into moments when you're actually doing your best. In CBT, we'd call that an automatic thought, and it's worth gently asking: what would you say to a close friend who was working full days *and* raising kids alone and still showing up every day? What evidence do you actually have, when you step back, that your son is not being cared for and loved?

client: I hear what you're saying, and I know logically that I'd tell a friend she was doing an amazing job... but it feels different when it's me. Like, I can see the evidence — he's fed, he's going to school, he laughs sometimes — but then I think, is that the bar? Just keeping him alive and functional? I guess I worry that "showing up" isn't the same as actually being present, and most nights I'm so exhausted I feel like I'm just going through the motions with him.
therapist: That distinction you're making — between showing up and truly being present — shows a really deep level of care for your son, and that awareness itself is something a disengaged parent simply wouldn't have. It's worth gently challenging the idea that "going through the motions" during an unusually hard stretch means that's who you are as a parent, rather than just what exhaustion looks like right now. Can you think of even one small moment recently — however brief — where you felt genuinely connected with him, not just functional?

client: I appreciate you saying that, but honestly it's hard to take in right now because the guilt kind of drowns everything else out. There was this one moment last week where he was showing me some drawing he made and I actually stopped what I was doing and we talked about it for a few minutes, and he seemed really happy. But then I immediately thought, "that's one moment out of how many where I was barely there," and it just made me feel worse somehow.
therapist: That moment with the drawing is actually really significant — you noticed him, you stopped, you connected, and he felt it. But what you're describing afterward is something we call "discounting the positive," where your mind almost punishes you for the good moment by immediately using it as evidence against yourself, which is such a painful pattern. What do you think it would feel like to let that moment just be what it was — a real, genuine connection — without it needing to "cancel out" anything?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it was just... a good moment, full stop. But it's hard because my brain immediately goes to "okay, but what about all the times you weren't present, all the times you were distracted or snappy or just not there for him." It feels almost dangerous to let myself feel good about one thing when there's this whole weight of evidence on the other side.
therapist: There's something really telling in the word you used — "dangerous" — like allowing yourself one moment of self-compassion might somehow let your guard down or mean you're not taking your shortcomings seriously enough. But I'd gently ask: do you think the relentless focus on every imperfect moment is actually making you a *better* parent, or is it mostly just keeping you exhausted and depleted? What do you think would happen if you allowed yourself to be a flawed, trying-hard, good-enough parent — what are you afraid that might mean?

client: I think you're right that it keeps me exhausted, but part of me genuinely believes that if I stop scrutinizing myself so hard, I'll just... slip. Like the guilt is the only thing keeping me accountable, and without it I might miss something important or make the same mistakes over and over. I'm afraid that "good enough" is just a polite way of saying I've given up on being the parent my kids actually deserve.
therapist: What you're describing is actually a really common and understandable belief — that guilt is the engine keeping you on track — but it's worth asking whether guilt is actually a reliable accountability system, or whether it mostly just punishes you after the fact without giving you any useful guidance. A caring inner voice that says "that moment was hard, how can I do it differently?" is actually far more useful for growth than one that simply catalogues your failures. What do you think *genuine* accountability — the kind that actually helps you improve — might feel like, if it didn't have to feel like suffering?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me gets it intellectually, but honestly? It's hard to imagine accountability without that sharp edge to it. Like, if I'm not feeling bad about the times I've let people down or pulled away when they needed me, what's actually stopping me from just... doing it again? The guilt feels like proof that I care, and without it I'm worried I'd just become someone who doesn't.
therapist: There's something really moving in what you just said — the idea that guilt is proof of love, that feeling bad is how you know you're still the person who cares. But I'd gently offer another possibility: the fact that you're here, in this conversation, working this hard to be better for your kids *is* the proof that you care — not the suffering itself. What if the caring was always yours to keep, and the guilt was just a story your mind attached to it to make it feel more real?

client: That's... a really different way of looking at it, and part of me wants to hold onto it. But honestly, it's hard to believe that just showing up here counts as proof, because it feels too easy — like I could be here and still be a terrible parent at the end of the day. The guilt at least feels like it's doing something, like it's keeping me accountable so I don't just let myself off the hook.
therapist: There's a quieter kind of struggle in what you're saying now — not panic, but this deep, stubborn resistance to letting yourself off the hook, like part of you has decided that ease itself is suspicious. But I want to reflect something back: you've described guilt as "doing something," yet everything you've told me today suggests it's mostly been draining you without actually changing your behavior — you're still showing up, still noticing, still trying, *despite* the guilt rather than because of it. What if the guilt isn't the engine you think it is, but more like a weight you've been carrying that's making the journey harder than it needs to be?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me actually wants to believe it. But I keep coming back to this fear that if I let go of the guilt, I'll just... stop caring, or stop trying to be a better friend to the people I've been neglecting. Like the guilt is the only thing keeping me tethered to the fact that I've let people down.
therapist: There's a quieter fear underneath what you're describing now — not just about parenting, but about your friendships too, like guilt has become the thread connecting you to everyone you care about. But I'd gently point out that someone who truly didn't care wouldn't feel this fear of losing the tether — the caring is already there, woven into the worry itself. What do you think it would actually look like, in a practical way, to stay connected to the people you love and the parent you want to be, if it came from intention rather than guilt?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it — that the worry itself means I care. But honestly, when I try to imagine connecting from "intention" instead of guilt, I don't even know what that looks like, because guilt has been the engine for so long that I'm not sure I'd reach out at all without it. Like, what if I took the guilt away and there was just... nothing there?
therapist: That fear — that without guilt there might be "nothing there" — is one of the most painful things a person can believe about themselves, and I want to sit with that for a moment because it takes real courage to say out loud. But I'd gently offer this: the fact that the idea of "nothing there" frightens you so much is itself evidence of something — a person who truly had nothing inside wouldn't be afraid of emptiness, they simply wouldn't care. What's one relationship or moment in your life where you acted out of something that felt like genuine warmth or love, before guilt had a chance to get involved?
